pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 1, Skippi Ice Pops took ₹1 crore for 15% equity — that one line is a ₹6.67 crore valuation. Revamp Moto gave only 1.5% for ₹1 crore, so its valuation was about ₹66.7 crore. Same cheque, wildly different value, and it all comes from one division. This free calculator does that division in rupees and crores so you can check any Shark Tank India deal yourself.
what: A Shark Tank India valuation calculator turns two numbers from a pitch — the amount invested and the equity given for it — into the valuation of the whole company. Investors call the answer the post-money valuation: the value of the business after the new money is in. The maths is a single division, but the number it produces is the one founders and sharks argue about for the whole episode.

The tool also shows the pre-money valuation (the value before the investment) and the stake the founder keeps. On Tank Metrics everything is shown in ₹ Lakhs and ₹ Crores, because that is how Indian founders, investors and chartered accountants actually talk. There is no dollar conversion and no US template in the way.

One more thing this calculator settles is the gap between what a founder asks for and what the sharks finally agree to. Most pitches open with a valuation claim and then settle lower once the equity is negotiated. Seeing both numbers side by side is how you learn to price a deal before you are in the room.

formula.note: Investment in ₹ crore, equity as a percentage. The result is the post-money valuation.

example.intro: Suppose your business makes ₹1.2 crore of profit a year and an investor offers ₹1 crore for 10%. Here is how the same deal reads at different stakes, in ₹ Crores.
example.outro: Notice how the same ₹10 crore valuation comes out of three very different offers. The last row is Skippi Ice Pops' real deal: ₹1 crore for 15%, which is ₹6.67 crore. That is why sharks look at the valuation before they look at the cheque.

steps: Step 1 - Enter the amount
Type the investment in ₹ crore or lakh. You can write 1 crore or 50 lakh and the field understands both.
Step 2 - Enter the equity
Type the equity percentage the investor is asking for. Example: 15%.
Step 3 - Read the valuation
The calculator shows post-money valuation, pre-money valuation and your remaining stake, all in ₹.
why_india: American valuation tools count in millions and billions; India counts in lakh and crore, and one crore is ten million. The same value reads as a very different number depending on the unit, which is exactly where founders get confused when they copy a US calculator.

Indian equity deals are usually issued as CCPS (Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares), and a valuation often has to be certified by a chartered accountant or a SEBI-registered merchant banker. That is a different system from the US 409A valuation, so an Indian founder needs a calculator that thinks in ₹ and in Indian deal terms.

Indian founders also raise from family and friends before any angel, and those early rounds are rarely written down with a formal valuation. When a later angel asks for equity, this calculator is how you turn an informal round into a real number you can defend in front of a chartered accountant.
faqs: How do you calculate a Shark Tank India valuation?
Use Valuation = (Investment ÷ Equity) × 100. If someone gives ₹1 crore for 10% equity, the valuation is ₹10 crore. Skippi Ice Pops gave 15% for ₹1 crore, so its valuation was ₹6.67 crore.
What is the difference between pre-money and post-money valuation?
Post-money is the value after the investment. Pre-money is post-money minus the investment. For ₹1 crore at 10%, post-money is ₹10 crore and pre-money is ₹9 crore.
Is this calculator free and does it show rupees?
Yes. The Tank Metrics Shark Tank valuation calculator is free and shows every figure in ₹ Lakhs and ₹ Crores, made for Indian founders.

pages.hook: On Shark Tank India, Revamp Moto gave just 1.5% for ₹1 crore, because its valuation was about ₹66.7 crore. The Sass Bar gave 35% for ₹50 lakh. Same show, and the equity for a rupee is not fixed at all — it depends entirely on what your company is worth. This calculator tells you the honest number for your business.
what: How much equity you give for ₹1 crore is decided by your valuation, not by the cheque size. If your company is worth ₹10 crore and you raise ₹1 crore, you should be giving about 10%. If it is worth ₹20 crore, the same ₹1 crore costs you only 5%. Raise the valuation and the equity for the same money falls.

Tank Metrics takes your valuation and returns the exact equity for ₹1 crore, plus what ₹50 lakh and ₹2 crore would cost you. It is the fastest way to answer a founder's real question: how much of my company am I actually selling for this money? Everything is shown in ₹ Lakhs and ₹ Crores.

There is also a practical floor to keep in mind. Investors rarely accept much below 1% for a meaningful cheque, because a tiny stake is hard to track and harder to sell later. So even a very high valuation has a minimum equity below which the deal stops making sense for the investor.

The cleanest way to hold your equity is to arrive at the negotiation with your own valuation already worked out from revenue and profit. A founder who can show the arithmetic keeps far more of the company than one who accepts the first percentage on the table.

formula.note: At a ₹20 crore valuation the equity is (1 ÷ 20) × 100 = 5%.

example.intro: Here is what ₹1 crore costs in equity at different valuations. Every row is the same cheque; only the valuation changes.
example.outro: The lesson is blunt: the stronger your valuation, the less equity the same money costs. Revamp Moto raised ₹1 crore at a ₹66.7 crore valuation and gave only 1.5%. Improving your valuation is the founder's real job, not haggling over the cheque.

steps: Step 1 - Enter your valuation
Type your company's current valuation in ₹ crore. If you do not know it, start from a profit or revenue multiple.
Step 2 - Pick the cheque
The calculator already shows ₹1 crore, ₹50 lakh and ₹2 crore so you can compare three rounds at once.
Step 3 - Read the equity
See exactly how much equity each cheque costs you at your valuation, and how much stake you keep.
why_india: In India an equity round is not just a percentage. Along with the equity come a board seat, veto rights and a liquidation preference, all of which sit on top of the headline number. A plain US calculator that returns only a percentage misses every one of those Indian deal layers.

For a small Indian business, angel investors are comfortable taking 10% to 20% for a ₹1 crore seed round. Once revenue and profit grow, the same cheque becomes 5% or even 2%. That shift is normal in India, and it is the reason valuation work pays for itself.

India also taxes a transfer differently from a fresh issue. A new issue of shares is not a taxable event for the founder, but a secondary sale of existing shares is, so the structure of the round quietly changes the real cost of the equity you give away.
faqs: How much equity should I give for ₹1 crore?
It depends on your valuation: Equity % = (1 crore ÷ valuation) × 100. At a ₹10 crore valuation it is 10%, at ₹20 crore it is 5%, and at ₹50 crore it is only 2%.
Is giving more equity ever fine?
Early on, 15-20% is normal because the investor takes real risk. But giving more than 30% for ₹1 crore is expensive for your long-term ownership.
Does giving equity take away my control?
Giving 10% does not by itself hand over control, but a board seat and veto rights can come with the deal. This calculator shows your remaining stake so you can plan.

pages.hook: The biggest myth about boAt and Shark Tank India is that boAt pitched on the show. It never did. boAt's co-founder Aman Gupta is a shark — he sits on the investor side and hears other founders pitch. Yet boAt is the perfect yardstick for every deal you see on the show, because its valuation shows what a real Indian brand is worth at scale.
what: boAt's parent company is Imagine Marketing. At its 2025 IPO filing, the company was valued at roughly ₹15,000 crore, on yearly revenue of about ₹3,000 crore. Aman Gupta and Sameer Mehta built it from 2016 into India's largest audio and wearable brand. That is a story of scale, not of a single cheque.

When a Shark Tank India founder asks for ₹10 crore, boAt at ₹15,000 crore is the other end of the scale. This calculator lets you put a revenue figure and a multiple together to see the same kind of valuation the market gives a real Indian company. The point is simple: valuation comes from revenue and profit, not from a story.

The calculator also exposes an uncomfortable truth. A brand with ₹1 crore of revenue at a 5x multiple is worth ₹5 crore, no matter how good the story is. Revenue is the input the market cannot argue with, and it is the one a founder can actually grow.

For a founder the lesson is to grow the input the multiple multiplies. A brand at ₹10 crore of revenue does not need a cleverer story to reach ₹50 crore of value at a 5x multiple; it needs five times the revenue. That is a harder but far more honest path than arguing for a higher multiple.

formula.note: Shark Tank deals often sit at 2x to 10x revenue. At boAt's scale the multiple is lower.

example.intro: Below is boAt's valuation next to typical Shark Tank India deals, all in ₹ Crores. Watch how the multiple behaves as revenue grows.
example.outro: boAt's ₹15,000 crore did not come from one pitch. It came from years of revenue and scale. A brand worth ₹5 crore on the show grows toward boAt's number through the same multiple applied to a much bigger revenue. So connect your valuation to your revenue, not to your story.

Type your annual revenue in ₹ crore. Use the last twelve months of sales.
Step 2 - Enter a multiple
Pick a multiple for your category: D2C around 4x, SaaS 6x-10x, hardware and audio 2x-4x.
Step 3 - Read the valuation
The calculator shows the implied valuation in ₹, the same way a market prices a real brand.
why_india: In India, hardware and D2C brands usually trade at a lower revenue multiple than US brands, because margins are thinner and competition is fierce. boAt's multiple sits in single digits for exactly that reason, while a US audio brand can command a premium. Copying a US multiple overstates an Indian valuation.

An Indian valuation also has to stand up to a chartered accountant and SEBI rules, and deals are often structured as CCPS. US tools work on 409A and on dollars, which do not translate cleanly. Tank Metrics keeps everything in ₹ Crores so the number is one an Indian investor will recognise.

Indian hardware brands also carry higher working capital and import costs, which pull the multiple down further. A brand that imports components pays customs duty and IGST before it sells a single unit, so the revenue that reaches the multiple is already carrying that drag.

pages.h1: Burn Rate Calculator for Startups India - Free Calculator in ₹
pages.hook: On Shark Tank India, the question founders get asked most often is not about valuation — it is "monthly burn kitna hai?" Sharks ask it because a great story with a broken burn is still a dead business. Skippi Ice Pops halved its burn after the show and then grew 40x. Your burn rate and your runway are the two numbers that decide how much time you really have.
what: Burn rate is how much cash your business spends each month beyond what it earns. There are two versions: gross burn, the total spend, and net burn, the spend minus income. Net burn is the honest number, because it is what actually drains your bank account every month.

If you spend ₹5 lakh a month and earn ₹2 lakh, your net burn is ₹3 lakh. If you have ₹30 lakh in the bank, you have ten months of runway. Tank Metrics shows both the net burn and the runway in ₹ Lakhs, the way an Indian founder checks their own account, not in dollars.

Runway is the second half of the same question. Burn tells you how fast the money is leaving; runway tells you how many months that leaves you. A founder who knows both can raise the next round from a position of strength instead of from panic.

A useful habit is to write the burn and the runway down on the first of every month, before the invoices arrive. It takes two minutes and it turns a vague worry into a number you can act on. Founders who do this catch a rising burn two or three months early, which is exactly the window where a small fix is still cheap.

formula.expr: Net Burn = Monthly Expenses − Monthly Income
formula.note: Runway in months = Cash in Bank ÷ Net Burn.

example.intro: Three Indian startups, three very different months, all measured in ₹ Lakhs.
example.outro: The last row is the goal: when income passes expenses, burn disappears and the business funds itself. Skippi did exactly this — it cut its burn in half and became sustainable, and the growth followed. Track your net burn every single month, small or large.

steps: Step 1 - Enter monthly income
Type this month's total income in ₹ lakh. Zero is fine if you are pre-revenue.
Step 2 - Enter monthly expenses
Add salaries, rent, marketing and taxes into one monthly figure in ₹ lakh.
Step 3 - Read burn and runway
The calculator shows net burn and how many months of cash you have left, in ₹ Lakhs.
why_india: An Indian startup carries monthly liabilities that US burn tools ignore: GST, TDS and PF payments. Left out of the expense figure, they make the burn look smaller than it is. Adding them back gives the true picture of an Indian founder's month.

In India, a runway of more than twelve months is considered safe, because closing a funding round here takes three to six months. A US benchmark of six months is too tight for India. Tank Metrics keeps the runway and the burn in rupees, with the Indian timeline in mind.

India also has strong seasonal cash swings. The festive months bring revenue and the months after bring returns and slower sales, so a single month's burn can flatter the picture. An average of three months gives a truer runway than any one month does.
faqs: How do you calculate burn rate?
Net Burn = Monthly Expenses − Monthly Income. If expenses are ₹5 lakh and income is ₹2 lakh, the net burn is ₹3 lakh a month.
How much runway should a startup have?
Indian startups should keep at least twelve months of runway, because a new round takes three to six months to close. Under six months is the danger zone.
What is the difference between gross burn and net burn?
Gross burn is the total spend; net burn is spend minus income. Net burn is the real number because it shows how fast your cash is falling.

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 3, Decode Age took ₹1.5 crore for 2.25% equity plus a 1% royalty until ₹1 crore was recouped. A royalty deal gives the shark downside protection and lets the founder keep more equity, but it also takes a slice of every month's sales. This calculator shows you the real break-even between a royalty deal and a plain equity deal, in ₹ Crores.
what: A royalty deal means the investor takes a smaller equity stake plus a percentage of sales (a royalty) until a fixed amount is recouped. After that, the royalty stops and only the equity remains. It became common on Shark Tank India from Season 3 as a way to close a gap when founders and sharks disagree on valuation.

A pure equity deal takes equity only. A royalty deal saves equity up front but charges your cash flow every month. Tank Metrics puts the two side by side so you can see how many months the royalty runs and what it costs in total, all in ₹ Lakhs and ₹ Crores.

The trade is simple to state. A royalty deal buys you a smaller equity cut today and charges you a monthly slice of sales until the recoup is complete. Whether that is cheap or expensive depends entirely on how fast your sales grow from here.

One rule of thumb helps here. If the royalty would take more than about three years to recoup at your current sales, the deal is leaning toward the investor. If it recoups in under a year, the founder is giving away cash that pure equity might have cost less to part with. The right answer sits between those two ends.

formula.expr: Months to Recoup = Recoup Amount ÷ (Monthly Sales × Royalty %)
formula.note: Effective cost = equity given + total royalty paid until the recoup is complete.

example.intro: Say your monthly sales are ₹20 lakh and you raise ₹1.5 crore. Here is how a royalty deal compares with a pure equity deal, in ₹ Crores.
example.outro: A royalty deal saves equity but charges your cash flow monthly. If sales grow, the recoup finishes faster; if they stall, the royalty runs longer and the total you pay can pass what pure equity would have cost. So run the numbers before you say yes.

steps: Step 1 - Enter the deal terms
Type the investment, the equity percentage and the royalty percentage the shark is asking.
Step 2 - Enter monthly sales
Type your current monthly sales in ₹ lakh so the calculator can size the royalty.
Step 3 - Read the break-even
See the monthly royalty and how many months it takes to recoup, in ₹.
why_india: Royalty deals took off in India from Season 3, when sharks felt founders were asking for too-high valuations. On the US Shark Tank, Kevin O'Leary is famous for royalty offers, but in India the recoup amount is set in rupees and the royalty runs against rupee sales.

In India a royalty payment also attracts TDS, and GST sits on the revenue itself, so the net cash flow differs from a US deal. US royalty calculators ignore these Indian layers. Tank Metrics keeps the whole comparison in ₹ Crores and in Indian tax terms.

India also treats the royalty differently for each side. It is an operating cost for the investor and revenue for the company, which is exactly why a royalty deal is usually structured with a recoup cap. That cap is the number to negotiate hardest.
faqs: What is a Shark Tank royalty deal?

In a royalty deal the investor takes less equity but also a percentage of sales (a royalty) until the invested amount is recouped. For example, ₹1.5 crore for 2.25% equity plus 1% royalty until ₹1 crore is recouped.
Is a royalty deal good or bad for a founder?

It depends. It can save equity if sales grow fast and the royalty ends soon. If sales are slow, the royalty runs long and the total cost can exceed a pure equity deal, so calculate the break-even first.
What happens after the royalty is recouped?
Once the recoup amount is fully paid, the royalty stops and the investor keeps only the equity. That is why the recoup time matters so much.

Formula
Months to Recoup = Recoup Amount ÷ (Monthly Sales × Royalty %). Total cost = equity + total royalty.
Ek example

Monthly sales ₹20 lakh aur 1% royalty par har mahine ₹20,000 royalty jaati hai. ₹1 crore recoup karne mein lagbhag 50 mahine lagte hain. Pure equity deal mein 15% dena padta, jo zyada mehnga ho sakta hai.

India mein royalty par TDS lagta hai aur GST revenue ko affect karta hai, isi liye net cash flow US se alag hota hai. Sahi picture ke liye Indian taxes ke saath calculate karo.

calculator.compute: function(e){var r=val(e,"rev"),p=val(e,"prof");var m=r?p/r*100:0;return{rows:[{l:"Net Profit Margin",v:pct(m)},{l:"Profit per ₹100 of sales",v:inr2(m)},{l:"Markup on Cost",v:pct(r-p?p/(r-p)*100:0)},{l:"Net Profit",v:inr(p)}]}}

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 2, a D2C brand walked in with ₹12 crore of revenue and walked out without a deal - because its margin was barely 4%. The sharks said the same thing every time: revenue is vanity, margin is sanity. A business that sells ₹1 crore and keeps ₹10 lakh is a very different animal from one that keeps ₹25 lakh on the same sales. This calculator turns your revenue and profit into the margin in rupees, so you know which animal you are.
what: A profit margin calculator in rupees takes two numbers every founder already has - what you sold, and what you kept - and tells you the margin in a way that makes sense in India: a percentage, plus the rupees of profit on every ₹100 of sales.

Margin is profit divided by revenue. ₹1 crore of sales with ₹10 lakh of profit is a 10% margin. The same ₹1 crore with ₹25 lakh of profit is 25%. Revenue alone hides the difference; the margin exposes it.

Founders mix up margin and markup constantly. A 25% margin is a 33% markup on cost, and quoting the wrong one in a pitch is how a good business looks dishonest. This calculator shows both, so you never mix them again.

formula.note: Net profit is what is left after every cost - goods, salaries, rent, ads, tax. ₹10 lakh of profit on ₹1 crore of revenue is a 10% margin. Markup is a different number: profit divided by cost, not by revenue.

example.intro: Here is the same business at different margins, all in ₹ Lakhs and Crores. Watch how the profit per ₹100 of sales changes while the revenue does not.
example.outro: The third row is the goal every founder should chase: the same ₹1 crore of sales, but 2.5 times the profit of the second row. Nothing about the revenue changed - only the margin. That is why investors ask for margin first and turnover second.

steps: Step 1 - Enter your revenue
Type the sales for the period, in ₹ lakh or crore. The field reads '1 crore' and '50 lakh' as well as plain numbers.
Step 2 - Enter your net profit
Type what is left after all costs. A loss is fine - enter it as a negative number and the margin turns negative.
Step 3 - Read the margin
You get the margin %, the profit per ₹100 of sales, the markup on cost and the profit itself, all in ₹.
why_india: American margin tools report in dollars and talk about 'gross margin' in a US accounting sense that does not match how an Indian small business keeps its books. An Indian founder thinks in ₹ Lakhs, adds GST separately, and wants the margin on the number they actually bill.

In India a trader, a D2C brand and a services firm all measure margin differently - the trader on landed cost, the brand on cost of goods plus marketplace fees, the agency on billable hours. The one thing they share is that the answer has to be in rupees, not in a spreadsheet column labelled in dollars.

Indian lenders and investors ask for the margin on the last twelve months, not a single month. Keep feeding this calculator each month's revenue and profit, and you will have the number ready before anyone asks for it.
mistakes: Confusing margin with markup. A 25% margin is a 33% markup on cost; quoting the wrong one in a pitch makes a good business look dishonest.
Calculating margin on revenue that still includes GST. Strip the tax out first or the margin is understated.
Looking at one good month. Margin swings with season, discounts and one-off costs, so judge it on a rolling twelve months.
faqs: How do I calculate profit margin in rupees?
Divide net profit by revenue and multiply by 100. ₹10 lakh of profit on ₹1 crore of revenue is (10,00,000 ÷ 1,00,00,000) × 100 = a 10% margin.
What is the difference between margin and markup?
Margin is profit divided by revenue; markup is profit divided by cost. A 25% margin is a 33% markup. Confusing the two is the most common mistake Indian founders make in a pitch.
Is a 10% profit margin good in India?
It depends on the business. A trading firm can survive on 5-10%; a D2C brand usually needs 20%+ to fund ads and returns. Compare against your own industry, not a generic number.

Net Profit Margin = (Net Profit ÷ Revenue) × 100. ₹1 crore ki sale pe ₹10 lakh profit matlab 10% margin. Same sale pe ₹25 lakh profit matlab 25% margin.

pages.title: Pre Money vs Post Money Valuation India Explained
pages.description: Pre money vs post money valuation explained for Indian founders. Enter the cheque and equity to see both numbers, in ₹ Crores, instantly and free.
pages.h1: Pre Money vs Post Money Valuation India - Free Calculator in ₹
pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 3, a founder said he was valued at ₹4 crore. A shark offered ₹1 crore for 20% and corrected him on camera: the post-money valuation is ₹5 crore, not ₹4 crore. The founder had quoted the pre-money number and forgotten that the cheque gets added on top. It is the single most common valuation mistake Indian founders make on TV - and in term sheets. This calculator shows both numbers, so you never confuse them again.
what: Pre-money and post-money are the two valuations of the same deal, separated by the investment. Post-money is what the company is worth after the cheque lands; pre-money is post-money minus the cheque. The investor's equity is always a slice of the post-money number, never the pre-money one.

Get the order wrong and the deal is mispriced. Offer ₹1 crore for 10% and the post-money is ₹10 crore; the pre-money is ₹9 crore. A founder who quotes ₹9 crore as the valuation has just handed the investor an extra ₹1 crore of value for free.

Every term sheet in India is written in pre-money, and every shark on TV speaks in post-money, which is exactly why the two get mixed up. This calculator keeps both in front of you at once, in ₹ Crores.

formula.note: The equity percentage is always taken on the post-money valuation. ₹1 crore for 10% gives a ₹10 crore post-money and a ₹9 crore pre-money. Quote the pre-money in the term sheet, but do the division on post-money.

example.intro: Same company, different cheques and stakes. Watch how pre-money and post-money move together, all in ₹ Crores.
example.outro: The first three rows are all the same ₹10 crore post-money - only the cheque and the stake change. The fourth row is a different, smaller company: a ₹5 crore post-money and a ₹4 crore pre-money, which is exactly the ₹4 crore the founder in the hook quoted.

steps: Step 1 - Enter the investment
Type the cheque in ₹ crore or lakh. Both '1 crore' and '50 lakh' work.
Step 2 - Enter the equity offered
Type the stake the investor is asking for, as a percentage.
Step 3 - Read both valuations
The calculator shows post-money, pre-money and the founder's remaining stake, all in ₹.
why_india: Indian term sheets are written in pre-money valuation, but Indian TV and most founders speak in post-money. The gap between the two is the cheque itself, and quoting the wrong one can cost a founder crores in a single conversation.

In India the equity is usually issued as CCPS (Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares), and the valuation often needs a chartered accountant or a SEBI-registered merchant banker to certify it. That is a different system from the US 409A valuation, and it makes the pre-money / post-money distinction a legal one, not just a maths one.

Indian early rounds are frequently raised from family and friends without a written valuation. When a later angel asks for equity, this calculator is how you turn that informal history into a pre-money and post-money number you can defend in front of your CA.
mistakes: Quoting the pre-money valuation as if it were the post-money, which gives the investor more equity than the deal intended.
Applying the equity percentage to the pre-money number. It is always applied to post-money.
Forgetting the ESOP pool, which is usually created before the round and sits inside the pre-money, quietly diluting founders.
faqs: What is the difference between pre-money and post-money valuation?
Post-money is the company's value after the investment; pre-money is post-money minus the investment. For ₹1 crore at 10%, post-money is ₹10 crore and pre-money is ₹9 crore.
Which valuation do Indian term sheets use?
Indian term sheets are normally written in pre-money valuation, while founders and TV pitches usually quote post-money. Always check which one a number refers to before agreeing.
Is the equity percentage calculated on pre-money or post-money?
Always on post-money. The investor's ₹1 crore is part of the ₹10 crore post-money company, so 10% is 10% of ₹10 crore, not of ₹9 crore.
hinglish_blocks: Pre-money aur post-money me farak
Post-money matlab investment ke baad company ki value; pre-money matlab post-money se investment ghataakar. Investor ko equity hamesha post-money par milti hai, pre-money par nahi.
Formula
Post-Money = (Investment ÷ Equity) × 100, aur Pre-Money = Post-Money − Investment. ₹1 crore ke 10% par post-money ₹10 crore, pre-money ₹9 crore.
Ek example
Shark Tank India Season 3 me founder ne ₹4 crore valuation bola, par ₹1 crore ke 20% par post-money ₹5 crore thi. Yahi galti term sheet me bhi aam hai.

Investment aur equity daalo, dono valuation ek saath ₹ Crores me dekh lo. Kuch bhi kahin nahi bheja jaata.
India me kya alag hai
Indian term sheet pre-money me likha jaata hai par pitch post-money me hoti hai. Equity CCPS par issue hoti hai aur valuation CA ya merchant banker certify karta hai.

calculator.name: LTV : CAC Ratio
calculator.compute: function(e){var l=val(e,"ltv"),c=val(e,"cac");var r=c?l/c:0;var v=r>=3?"Healthy (3:1 or better)":r>=1?"Watch (under 3:1)":"Losing money (below 1:1)";return{rows:[{l:"LTV : CAC",v:num(r,2)+" : 1"},{l:"Verdict",v:v},{l:"Lifetime Value",v:inr(l)},{l:"Acquisition Cost",v:inr(c)}]}}

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 3, a D2C brand came with a confident pitch about growth and repeat buyers. Then a shark asked the one question that ends most pitches: what is your LTV to CAC? The founder did not have the number. Every rupee spent winning a customer has to come back several times over for growth to build a business instead of burning one. This calculator gives you that number for your D2C or SaaS business in seconds, in ₹.
what: The LTV:CAC ratio puts two numbers side by side: what a customer is worth to you over their whole life (LTV), and what it cost to win them (CAC). Divide one by the other and you get the single figure investors in Indian D2C and SaaS ask for first.

A ratio of 3:1 or better is the common rule of thumb. Below 1:1 you lose money on every customer you win; between 1 and 3 you are spending too much to grow. A D2C brand with an LTV of ₹4,500 and a CAC of ₹1,500 is at 3:1 - healthy. A quick-commerce brand with ₹800 of LTV and ₹1,200 of CAC is at 0.67:1 - it loses money on every order.

The ratio only means something when both sides are measured the same way. LTV should be built on gross-margin profit, not revenue, and CAC should include ads, salaries and agency fees - not just the ad bill. Measure one side generously and the other tightly and the ratio lies.

formula.expr: LTV : CAC = Lifetime Value ÷ Customer Acquisition Cost
formula.note: Use profit-based LTV and fully-loaded CAC. An LTV of ₹4,500 over a ₹1,500 CAC gives 3 : 1. Below 1:1 the business loses money on every customer; 3:1 and above is the range investors look for.

example.intro: Three Indian businesses, three very different ratios, all in ₹. Watch how the verdict changes even when the LTV looks large.
example.outro: The quick-commerce row is the trap: a real customer, real revenue, and still a loss on every single one. That is why a large LTV is not enough on its own - the ratio is what tells you whether growth is building the business or eating it.

steps: Step 1 - Enter lifetime value
Type what one customer is worth over their whole relationship, in ₹ - use profit, not revenue.
Step 2 - Enter acquisition cost
Type the fully-loaded cost of winning one customer: ads, sales salaries, agency fees.
Step 3 - Read the ratio and verdict
The calculator shows the LTV:CAC ratio and labels it healthy, watch or losing money.
why_india: Indian D2C founders usually track revenue and order counts, not unit economics, because that is what the marketplace dashboard shows. The LTV:CAC ratio forces the two numbers that decide survival onto one screen.

Indian SaaS companies often bill in dollars but pay for talent and ads in rupees, so the ratio gets distorted if the two sides are converted carelessly. Keep both sides in ₹ over the same period and the number is honest.

Indian investors have become far stricter about this ratio since the funding winter - a 1.2:1 pitch that raised money in 2021 does not raise it now. Having the number ready, and honest, is the difference between a second meeting and a polite no.
mistakes: Using revenue-based LTV against a fully-loaded CAC, which makes a loss-making business look healthy.
Leaving sales salaries and agency fees out of CAC, so the cost of winning a customer looks far lower than it is.
Using a blended CAC that hides a channel where you lose money on every single customer.
faqs: What is a good LTV to CAC ratio in India?
3:1 or better is the usual rule. Below 1:1 you lose money on every customer; between 1 and 3 you are spending too much to grow. Low-margin businesses need a higher ratio than sticky ones.
How do I calculate LTV for an Indian D2C brand?
Average order value × purchases per year × customer lifespan in years × gross margin %. Use profit, not revenue, or the ratio overstates what a customer is worth.
What should CAC include?
Every cost of winning a customer: ad spend, the sales team's salaries, agency fees and introductory discounts - divided by the new customers won in the same period.

LTV : CAC = Lifetime Value ÷ Acquisition Cost. ₹4,500 LTV pe ₹1,500 CAC matlab 3:1 - healthy. 1:1 se neeche har customer pe nuksaan.
Ek example

pages.description: Free dilution calculator for founders. Enter your equity, each round and the ESOP pool to see exactly how much of your company you keep.
pages.h1: Dilution Calculator for Founders - Free Calculator in ₹

calculator.name: Founder Dilution
calculator.compute: function(e){var b=val(e,"before"),g=val(e,"give"),s=val(e,"esop");var after=b*(1-g/100)*(1-s/100);return{rows:[{l:"Founder Equity After",v:pct(after)},{l:"Investor Stake",v:pct(b)},{l:"ESOP Pool",v:pct(s)},{l:"Equity You Gave Up",v:pct(b-after)}]}}

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 1, a founder gave away 20% for ₹1 crore and felt lucky. Two years later a second round took another 20%, and an ESOP pool for senior hires took 10% more. The founder who once owned the whole company was now under 60% - and had never once sat down and multiplied it out. Dilution compounds, and each round is charged against a smaller and smaller base. This calculator shows what you keep after the round, the ESOP pool, and the rupees of company you actually gave up.
what: Dilution is the slice of the company a founder gives away, and the slice that is left. If you own 100% today and hand an investor 10%, you keep 90%. That part is simple - the part that catches founders out is what happens across several rounds and an ESOP pool.

Dilution compounds because each round is charged against a smaller base. Lose 10% in round one and you are at 90%. Lose 20% in round two and you are at 72%, not 70%. Add a 10% ESOP pool and you are at 64.8%. A founder who started with everything can end up below two-thirds without a single round looking large.

The number that matters is not the stake alone but the stake next to the valuation. Giving 20% at a high price can cost less of the company's value than giving 5% at a low one. This calculator shows the stake after the round, the ESOP pool, and the total equity given up, so the trade-off is visible before the term sheet is signed.

formula.expr: Founder Equity After = Equity Before × (1 − Equity Given ÷ 100) × (1 − ESOP Pool ÷ 100)
formula.note: Multiply, do not subtract, across rounds. 100% after a 10% round is 90%; a further 20% round leaves 72%, not 70%. The ESOP pool dilutes founders exactly like an investor does.

example.intro: One founder, three dilutive events, all in percentages. Watch how the multiplication - not subtraction - decides what is left.
example.outro: Notice the second row: a 20% round off 90% leaves 72%, not the 70% most founders calculate in their head. That 2% is a real slice of a real company. By the last row, three rounds that each looked modest have taken more than a third of the business.

steps: Step 1 - Enter your current equity
Type the stake you hold today as a percentage - 100% if this is the first round.
Step 2 - Enter the equity given and the ESOP pool
Type the stake this round takes and any option pool created alongside it.
Step 3 - Read what you keep
The calculator shows your equity after the round, the investor stake, the ESOP pool and the total you gave up.
why_india: Indian founder agreements often create the ESOP pool before the round rather than after, which means the pool dilutes the founders and not the incoming investor. That ordering is a real difference from many US deals and it changes the final number.

Indian rounds frequently use CCPS (Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares) with anti-dilution clauses, and a down round can trigger them - meaning the founder's dilution is larger than the headline percentage suggests.

Indian family businesses that bring in an outside investor rarely write down how the founding family's stake will move across future rounds. This calculator is how you show your CA and your family exactly where the stake lands.
mistakes: Subtracting percentages across rounds instead of multiplying fractions, which understates the total dilution.
Forgetting the ESOP pool, which dilutes founders exactly like an investor does and is often created before the round.
Watching the stake and ignoring the valuation - giving 20% at a high price can cost less than 5% at a low one.
faqs: How do I calculate founder dilution?
Multiply, do not subtract. Equity after a round = equity before × (1 − equity given). 100% after a 10% round is 90%; a further 20% round leaves 72%.
Does the ESOP pool dilute founders?
Yes. The employee option pool is carved out of the cap table and dilutes founders exactly like an investor's stake does, unless the deal says otherwise.
How much dilution is normal per round in India?
Seed rounds typically take 10-20%, Series A another 15-25%. Across three rounds a founder can end up holding 50-65% of the company, which is normal and not a failure.

pages.h1: EMI Calculator for 2 Lakh Loan - Free Calculator in ₹
pages.hook: ₹2 lakh is the most common loan in India - a bike, a laptop for a new business, a small stock order, a wedding, a medical bill. And the question is always the same: kitni EMI padegi? A ₹2 lakh loan at 10% for two years is about ₹9,229 a month, and you repay roughly ₹221,500 in total - about ₹21,500 of that is pure interest. The rate and the tenure decide the EMI, and one year of extra tenure can quietly add lakhs to what you pay back. This calculator shows all of it in ₹.
what: An EMI - Equated Monthly Instalment - is a fixed amount you pay every month that covers both the interest on a loan and a part of the principal. It stays the same each month even though the split between interest and principal keeps shifting in favour of the principal as the loan runs down.

For a ₹2 lakh loan the EMI depends on two things: the annual interest rate and the tenure. At 10% over one year the EMI is about ₹17,584; stretch the same loan to two years and the EMI drops to ₹9,229, but the total interest almost doubles to about ₹21,500. A longer tenure means a smaller monthly bite and a bigger total bill.

This calculator shows the monthly EMI, the total interest, the total payment and the principal, all in ₹. Enter any amount, rate or tenure - the ₹2 lakh default is just the most common starting point - and the numbers update instantly.

formula.note: P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100) and n is the tenure in months. A ₹2 lakh loan at 10% for 24 months gives an EMI of about ₹9,229.

example.intro: The same ₹2 lakh loan at four different rates and tenures, all in ₹. Watch the EMI fall and the total interest rise as the tenure grows.
example.outro: The last two rows share a tenure and differ only in the rate - and a 2% higher rate adds about ₹7,000 to what you repay on a ₹2 lakh loan. The EMI looks almost the same; the total does not. Always compare loans on the total interest, not just the monthly figure.

steps: Step 1 - Enter the loan amount
Type ₹2 lakh, or any amount - the calculator handles any loan size.
Step 2 - Enter the rate and tenure
Type the annual interest rate and the tenure in months. Both are on your sanction letter.
Step 3 - Read the EMI and total
You get the monthly EMI, the total interest, the total payment and the principal, all in ₹.
why_india: Indian lenders quote an annual reducing-balance rate, but many borrowers still compare offers on the flat rate, which understates the true cost. The EMI formula here uses the reducing-balance method that banks actually charge, so the total interest is the real one.
Indian loans often carry processing fees, insurance and GST on the fee, which are not part of the EMI but do raise the effective cost. Add those to the total payment to see what the loan truly costs.

A 2 lakh loan is small enough that the rate difference between a bank, an NBFC and a fintech app can be several percentage points. On a short tenure that difference is small; on a longer one it is a real amount of money, which is why comparing the total matters.
mistakes: Comparing loans on the flat rate instead of the reducing-balance rate - the flat rate hides a much higher true cost.
Choosing the longest tenure just because the EMI is smallest, and paying far more interest in total.
Forgetting processing fees, insurance and GST, which raise the effective cost above the quoted rate.
faqs: What is the EMI for a 2 lakh loan?
It depends on the rate and tenure. At 10% for 24 months the EMI is about ₹9,229; at 10% for 12 months it is about ₹17,584. Use the calculator above for your exact rate and tenure.
How is EMI calculated?
EMI = P × r × (1 + r)ⁿ ÷ ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1), where P is the loan, r the monthly rate and n the number of months. The same formula is used by every Indian bank.
Does a longer tenure reduce the total cost?
No. A longer tenure lowers the monthly EMI but raises the total interest you pay. On a ₹2 lakh loan at 10%, moving from 12 to 24 months roughly doubles the interest.
